column4: This is the section's exact acoustic counterpart: on the summoning Day voices خَشَعَتْ before the Merciful and the hearer detects only a whisper, turning the bowed face of 88:2 into bowed sound.
Paradise contains no heard لَغْوًا, only سَلَامًا; it states both the excluded speech and the word that replaces it in the section's protected soundscape.
The blessed hear neither لَغْوًا nor speech that incurs sin, precisely expanding the kind of word excluded by 88:11.
After 56:25 removes vain and sinful speech, this ayah supplies the audible remainder, “peace, peace,” so Paradise's silence is shown to be purification rather than muteness.
In the Garden they hear neither لَغْوًا nor denial or lying; the second exclusion sharpens the section's gloss of لاغية as morally ugly speech.
Paradise drinking produces neither لَغْوٌ nor sin-incurring talk, another direct formulation of an environment cleansed of corrupt speech.
Unbelievers command one another not to listen to the Quran and to make noise, وَٱلْغَوْا فِيهِ; earthly noise is used to block the revealed report that Paradise later excludes as لغو.
When believers hear ٱللَّغْوَ they turn away and answer with peace; their earthly discipline joins the section's two Paradise motifs, exclusion of vain speech and the hearing of salām.
God makes the saving event a تَذْكِرَةً and an attentive ear retains it; this is the section's whole passage from narrated news through hearing to awakened memory.
God sends down “the best حديث”; skins shiver and then hearts soften to God's remembrance, joining revealed report, fearful bodily humility, and ذكر in one response.
Each people rejects its arriving messenger and is then made أَحَادِيثَ; it exactly realizes the section's warning that a hearer of the report can become a cautionary report.
After the people reject their provision and are scattered, God makes them أَحَادِيثَ, the precise dictionary branch in which destroyed people become exemplary tales.
وَهَلْ أَتَىٰكَ حَدِيثُ مُوسَىٰ is the same address and formula as 88:1, here opening a past story delivered to the Prophet.
هَلْ أَتَىٰكَ حَدِيثُ مُوسَىٰ repeats the section's question almost verbatim and again makes a past story arrive as heard revelation.
هَلْ أَتَىٰكَ حَدِيثُ ضَيْفِ إِبْرَاهِيمَ opens Abraham's guest story with the same report-reaching-the-addressee formula.
هَلْ أَتَىٰكَ حَدِيثُ ٱلْجُنُودِ opens the Pharaoh and Thamud recollection with the same formula, making ruined peoples into the report now heard.
“Has there not come to you the news” of Noah, ʿĀd, and Thamud asks later hearers to receive destroyed peoples as warning, a nonlexical match for the opening and the “become reports” motif.
“Has the news not come to you” of earlier unbelievers is immediately followed by the evil consequence they tasted, making reception of old news a warning about the hearer's own future.
The question whether news of earlier peoples reached them introduces successive destroyed communities, directly joining transmitted history to the danger of repeating it.
أَتَىٰ أَمْرُ ٱللَّهِ speaks of God's still-awaited command as already arrived and then forbids haste, the clearest parallel to 88's future Day told as arrived news.
The promise that God will gather everyone on Resurrection Day ends by asking who is truer than God in حَدِيثًا; future judgment is guaranteed as truthful report.
The disputed ٱلنَّبَإِ ٱلْعَظِيمِ is the coming resurrection, another future overwhelming event presented to present hearers as “the great news.”
The Prophet is not a compeller over them and must remind with the Quran whoever fears the warning, almost exactly combining 88:21's task with 88:22's limit.
The Prophet's duty is only delivery while accounting belongs to God; this anticipates the exact division at 88:21–26 between reminder and divine reckoning.
The jinn listen to the Quran, command silence, and then return to warn their people; a first audience becomes the next bearer of the heard report.
The returning jinn say they heard a revealed book confirming Moses and guiding to truth, giving the content they transmit after the listening scene of 46:29.
They call their people to answer God's caller and believe, completing the section's movement from receiving a report to placing it in other ears.
People in the Fire say that had they truly listened or reasoned they would not be its inhabitants; سماع here plainly means receptive understanding, not sound alone.
Whenever a newly renewed reminder, ذِكْرٍ مِّن رَّبِّهِم مُّحْدَثٍ, comes, they listen while playing; the ayah fuses the ح د ث, س م ع, and ذ ك ر lines while exposing failed reception.
Every newly renewed reminder from the Merciful reaches them only for them to turn away, linking incoming speech, ذكر, and refusal to hear it responsively.
God says, “Our signs came to you and you forgot them”; أَتَتْكَ and نَسِيتَهَا reverse the section's opening reception and closing command to make the report remembered.
Believers are asked whether it is time for their hearts to become humble, تَخْشَعَ, to God's remembrance and revealed truth; heard reminder should produce inward khushūʿ.
Those given knowledge fall on their faces weeping as recitation increases their خُشُوعًا, connecting revealed words with the bodily humility whose acoustic form the section hears.
When the Quran is recited, hearers are commanded to listen and be silent; this is voluntary, attentive silence before revelation rather than the frightened hush of 20:108.
The messengers' stories contain a lesson and are not حَدِيثًا يُفْتَرَىٰ; the ayah marks the transmitted story as truthful revelation meant to instruct its hearer.
The Prophet nearly consumes himself with grief if people do not believe “this حديث”; against that burden, 88:21 defines his role as giving the reminder.
God tells the Prophet to leave to Him whoever denies “this حديث”; the revealed report is the Prophet's to deliver, while requital remains God's work.
The guided servants listen to “the word” and follow its best, a direct enactment of سماع as comprehension and obedience rather than bare audition.
Protection is granted so a seeker may hear كَلَامَ ٱللَّهِ and reach safety; revelation literally reaches a human through the ear before a response is possible.
A party hears God's word, understands it, and then knowingly distorts it, explicitly separating physical hearing, understanding, and obedient fidelity.
Some listen to the Prophet but leave asking what he just said; the heard sound fails to become understanding or retained reminder.
The preceding ruined peoples are a reminder for one who has a heart or “casts the ear” attentively, making past news effective only through present receptive hearing.
Moses is chosen and told to listen to what is revealed, a direct instance of speech reaching its first addressee by revelation and audition.
The Prophet is told by revelation that a group of jinn listened and said they had heard a wondrous Quran; hearing becomes both their testimony and fresh revealed news.
The one reminded of God's signs turns away and forgets his own deeds while deafness covers his ears, bringing reminder, forgetting, and failed hearing together.
The servants of the Merciful do not meet reminder of God's signs as if deaf and blind, defining remembrance as alert reception.
فَذَكِّرْ repeats 88:21's command to remind and makes the benefit of reminder the criterion for the prophetic address.
The person who fears will remember, identifying the receptive hearer for the command in 87:9 and for the reminder in this section.
The direct command وَذَكِّرْ says reminder benefits believers, closely matching the closing commission of 88:21.
Warning benefits the one who follows the reminder and fears the Merciful unseen, specifying the hearer whom prophetic speech can actually move.
The Quran is sent as a تَذْكِرَةً for one who fears, so the same surah that asks about Moses' report first defines revelation as fear-awakening reminder.
God promises to make the Prophet recite so that he will not forget, joining oral transmission with the memory required of the first recipient.
God makes the revelation easy on the Prophet's tongue so that people may remember, directly tracing the section's movement from speech on a tongue to memory in listeners.
The news of the messengers is related to steady the Prophet's heart, and in it truth, admonition, and reminder have come to him; received story becomes stabilizing proclamation.
After Moses' story, God says He relates earlier news to the Prophet and has given him a ذكر, explicitly naming story-report and reminder as one revelatory task.
Noah's account is called unseen news revealed to the Prophet, which neither he nor his people knew; revelation is the route by which the report reaches him.
Joseph's account is unseen news revealed to the Prophet, who was absent from the scene; the ayah distinguishes transmitted revelation from eyewitness knowledge.
Mary's story is unseen news revealed to the Prophet, who was not present at the casting of lots; the absent event reaches him as report.
وَهَلْ أَتَىٰكَ نَبَؤُا ٱلْخَصْمِ uses the same question and addressee as 88:1 with نبأ instead of حديث, then opens a narrated encounter.
God recites to the Prophet some of the news of Moses and Pharaoh in truth for believing hearers, making old events present through revelation.
Revelation descends upon the Prophet's heart “so that you may be one of the warners”; the recipient of divine speech is thereby made its transmitter.
The Reminder is sent down to the Prophet so he may explain to people what was sent to them, a direct relay from first addressee to subsequent hearers.
The ayah identifies revelation, speech from behind a veil, and a sent messenger as God's modes of speaking to a human, grounding the section's definition of words arriving through revelation.
God says He revealed a spirit from His command to the Prophet and made it light for guidance, applying the revelatory mode named in 42:51 to this messenger.
On the coming Day no soul speaks except by God's permission, a direct Judgment scene in which ordinary human speech falls silent.
“This is a day when they will not speak” gives an uncompromising Judgment silence parallel to the voices hushed in the section.
They are not permitted to offer excuses, explaining the specific denied speech behind the silence stated in 77:35.
On the Day the Spirit and angels stand in ranks, none speaks except one permitted by the Merciful who says what is right; silence has a divinely bounded exception.
The trumpet is blown and the criminals are gathered, supplying the announced setting for the lowered voices and following of the caller in 20:108.
The gathered people whisper among themselves about how briefly they stayed, an adjacent low-voiced exchange that prepares the “only a whisper” soundscape of 20:108.
Immediately after the hush of 20:108, intercession itself is restricted to one permitted by the Merciful and acceptable in speech, defining the boundary on utterance.
On Judgment Day those who disobeyed the Messenger wish to be levelled with the earth yet cannot conceal from God حَدِيثًا; the hearer's response has become an inescapable reported fact.
With eyes خُشَّعًا people emerge from graves and move toward the caller, joining bodily humility to the same summoned Judgment scene as the silenced voices of 20:108.
When Hell is brought near, the human remembers, but the ayah asks what use that remembrance can then have; it is the too-late counterpart to the present command to remind.
On the Day the human will remember what he strove for, showing the final involuntary recollection toward which the present reminder points.
As people are thrown into Hell, its keepers ask whether a warner had come to them; their present fate is explicitly measured against earlier reception of warning.
They confess that a warner did come but they denied him, supplying the rejected report whose failure to be heard leads to 67:10's regret.
At Hell's gates the keepers ask whether messengers came reciting signs and warning of this very meeting; the future report has become the hearer's present scene.
Humans and jinn are asked whether messengers from among them related God's signs and warned of this Day; they testify against themselves that the report did reach them.
After Noah's destruction, the Quran is said to be made easy for remembrance and asks whether anyone will remember, turning the narrated people into warning for a new hearer.
After ʿĀd's fate, the repeated invitation to remember makes the old catastrophe a present test of reception.
After Thamud's fate, the same refrain offers the transmitted story as an accessible reminder before its hearer repeats it.
After Lot's people, the final repeated refrain again joins a destroyed people's news to the audience's opportunity to remember.
The prayer and greeting of Paradise's people are glorification, peace, and praise, specifying wholesome words heard where vain speech is absent.
Angels enter upon the people of Eden saying “Peace be upon you” for their patience, giving the Garden's audible replacement for ugly speech.
Those admitted to gardens greet one another there with سَلَامٌ, directly populating the section's purified soundscape.
Angels take the good while saying “Peace be upon you; enter the Garden,” so salām is heard at the very threshold of Paradise.
The people admitted to bliss are guided to pure speech, ٱلطَّيِّبِ مِنَ ٱلْقَوْلِ, positively naming the kind of utterance that replaces لاغية.
The patient servants are rewarded with the high chamber and met there with greeting and peace, another Paradise scene filled with salutary speech.
The believers' greeting on the Day they meet God is سَلَامٌ, making peace the eschatological word of welcome.
سَلَامٌ قَوْلًا مِّن رَّبٍّ رَّحِيمٍ makes peace a spoken word from the Merciful Himself within Paradise.
At Paradise's opened gates its keepers say “Peace be upon you; you have done well; enter,” contrasting the received words at Hell's gates in 39:71.
The believers answer revelation with سَمِعْنَا وَأَطَعْنَا, making hearing explicitly culminate in obedience as the section's dictionary sense requires.
When called to God and His Messenger, believers say “We hear and we obey,” a direct formula for responsive rather than merely acoustic hearing.
The covenantal answer “We hear and obey” connects receiving spoken command with the obedience implicit in سماع.
Only those who truly hear respond, while the dead await resurrection; the ayah turns hearing into spiritual receptivity with final consequences.
The travelers have ears “with which to hear,” yet the real blindness belongs to hearts; the ayah explicitly relocates meaningful hearing from organ to understanding.
When they hear what was revealed to the Messenger, their eyes overflow because they recognize truth; heard revelation produces comprehension and bodily response.
When the Quran is recited, those given prior knowledge fall on their faces in prostration, an embodied answer to the arriving word that leads into 17:109's khushūʿ.
When the Merciful's signs are recited, the prophets and chosen ones fall prostrate and weeping; reception of the report becomes humble action.
The Messenger's duty is only conveyance while God knows what people disclose and hide, a concise parallel to “you are only a reminder.”
If the audience turns away, it must know that the Messenger's duty is only clear delivery, preserving the boundary between speaking and controlling response.
After the invitation to submit, the Prophet is told that if they turn away his duty is only conveyance, matching the limited commission at 88:21–22.
If they turn away, the Prophet's duty remains only clear conveyance; the hearer's refusal does not enlarge the messenger's authority.
The Messenger bears his assigned duty, the audience bears its own, and his obligation is only clear conveyance, sharply separating report from response.
After peoples before them denied, the ayah says the Messenger's duty is only clear conveyance, linking the recurring rejection stories to his present role.
The town's messengers say their duty is only clear conveyance, the same stance voiced collectively inside a cautionary story.
If they turn away, the Prophet was not sent as their guardian; upon him is only conveyance, closely restating both 88:21 and 88:22.
If people turn away, the Messenger's duty is only clear conveyance, another exact boundary around transmitted speech.
After signs in creation and the possibility that their term is near, the ayah asks what حديث after this they will believe, treating the revelation as the decisive warning discourse.
God's signs are recited in truth and the hearers are asked what حديث after God and His signs they will believe, defining the revealed report against rival speech.
The warning surah ends by asking what حديث after it they will believe, placing responsibility on the audience that has just heard the coming Day narrated.
The audience is asked whether it marvels at “this حديث,” identifying the recited warning itself as the report that now demands a humbled response.
The hearers are asked whether they treat “this حديث” lightly, exposing a dismissive response to the revealed report within a surah that also describes Paradise's purified hearing.
Deniers are challenged to produce a حديث like the revelation if truthful, marking this heard discourse as inimitable rather than ordinary talk.
When God's signs are heard being denied and mocked, believers must leave until the mockers enter another حديث; the ayah distinguishes revealed speech from corrupt talk surrounding it.
The Prophet must turn away when people plunge mockingly into God's signs until they enter a different حديث, guarding the setting in which revelation is heard.

A private حديث passes from the Prophet to a wife, is disclosed, and is then made known to him by God; it concretely shows speech traveling by hearing and by revelation, with disclosure as its moral boundary.
Believers turn away from ٱللَّغْوِ, practicing in earthly life the exclusion of vain speech that characterizes the Garden.
The servants of the Merciful do not witness falsehood and pass by ٱللَّغْوِ with dignity, defining a present relation to the speech absent in Paradise.
The good word is likened to a firmly rooted, fruit-bearing tree; it supplies a positive moral image for speech where the section excludes the ugly word.
God says the condemned are “forgotten” that Day as they forgot meeting it, an eschatological reversal of the reminder they failed to retain.
Those who forgot the meeting of their Day are told that they are now forgotten, showing the consequence of letting warning fail to become remembrance.
Because they forgot the meeting of the Day and rejected the signs, God “forgets” them that Day; ignored report becomes realized judgment.
When people forget what they were reminded of, ease is opened until sudden seizure, so failure to retain warning turns its audience into a cautionary story.
When the wrongdoers forget what they were reminded of, those forbidding evil are saved and the offenders seized, tying remembrance to survival within narrated history.
Joseph says “mention me” to the king, but Satan makes the man forget that mention; one ayah holds ذكر as spoken mention and as the opposite of forgetting.
“Remember your Lord when you forget” states exactly the dictionary opposition the section uses to explain the reminder's work in its listener.
لَهْوَ ٱلْحَدِيثِ is purchased to mislead people from God's way; this diverting discourse is the moral opposite of the truthful حديث meant to be heard and remembered.
On that Day mouths are sealed while hands speak and feet testify; it reverses ordinary speech and shows that silencing human voices cannot silence the truth of their deeds.
The answer “we hear and disobey” severs audition from obedience, directly marking the failed sense of سماع against the section's fuller definition.
“سمعنا وعصينا” and the hostile “hear, may you not be heard” corrupt both listening and address, a precise negative boundary around morally sound hearing.
The audience is forbidden to say “we have heard” while they do not truly hear, distinguishing claimed audition from receptive understanding.
Even if God made the unreceptive hear, they would turn away, so sound reception alone is exposed as insufficient without willing obedience.
When the Quran is recited to them they do not prostrate, reversing the humble embodied listening shown in 17:107–109 and 19:58.
Those whose eyes were veiled from God's reminder could not bear to hear, the negative union of blocked ذكر and blocked سماع.
Some listen to the Prophet while veils cover their hearts and deafness their ears; the ayah separates audible exposure from understanding the report.
Veils over hearts and heaviness in ears prevent understanding during Quranic recitation, so listeners turn away when God's oneness is mentioned.
The Quran is guidance and healing for believers but deafness to unbelievers, as though they are called from far away; one report becomes intelligible or inaudible according to reception.
Some listen to the Prophet, yet he cannot make the deaf hear when they do not understand; this limits the reminder's power over its audience.
The Prophet cannot make the dead or the retreating deaf hear the call, a direct boundary around his commission to speak the reminder.
The repeated statement that the Prophet cannot make the dead or retreating deaf hear defines nonresponse as beyond the speaker's control.
God makes whom He wills hear, while the Prophet cannot make those in graves hear; the giver of effective hearing is distinguished from the human reminder.
The question whether the Prophet can make the deaf hear or guide the plainly astray reinforces that his task is delivery, not control of reception.
An evil word is like an uprooted tree with no stability, the direct moral opposite of the good word and a concrete image for the ugly speech absent from the Garden.
God does not love evil speech voiced publicly except by one wronged, defining an earthly boundary around the kind of ugly utterance Paradise excludes altogether.
Immediately after the absence of لغو in 52:23, Paradise's people turn to one another and ask questions; their conversation shows that the promise removes corrupt speech rather than all speech.
Here اللَّغْوِ in oaths is unintentional or ineffective speech for which God does not take people to account; this different legal sense marks a semantic boundary from 88:11's ugly utterance.
God does not take people to account for اللَّغْوِ in oaths but does for deliberate oaths; intention distinguishes this use from the foul or vain speech excluded in Paradise.
The wrongdoers will hear and see with startling clarity when they come to God, although today they are plainly astray; the future scene reverses present failed perception.
People's reckoning has drawn near while they remain heedless and turn away, another way the coming Day is treated as imminent while its hearers fail to respond.
The Hour has drawn near, making the future event grammatically immediate in the same direction as 88's already-arrived report.
The Hour can only come suddenly, yet its signs have already come; present evidence makes the future warning already operative.
The approaching event has drawn near and none but God can uncover it, another compact announcement of the future as already at hand.
The opening question “about what are they asking one another?” makes a heard dispute the doorway to the great resurrection-news named in 78:2.
Earlier messengers endured denial until God's help came, and some of their news has reached the Prophet; received report steadies the new bearer against rejection.
The Prophet is commanded to recite Noah's news to the people, explicitly turning an old event into spoken warning for a new audience.
The command to recite Abraham's news makes the messenger voice a past story for present hearers, paralleling the report openings gathered in the section.
God says He relates the Companions' news to the Prophet in truth, another revealed story that reaches one addressee for proclamation.
Pharaoh's people are made a precedent and example for later peoples; without using أحاديث, it develops the same transformation of judged hearers into exemplary history.
If the Quran descended on a mountain it would be seen خَاشِعًا and split from fear, extending the section's humbled face and voice to creation's response to revelation.
The condemned are shown humbled, خَاشِعِينَ مِنَ ٱلذُّلِّ, looking furtively at the Fire; it shares the Judgment posture behind the section's bowed faces and voices.
On the Day their eyes are humbled and abasement covers them, a close visual parallel to the faces خاشعة in 88:2 whose acoustic counterpart the prose develops.
They emerge rapidly with eyes humbled and humiliation covering them, another summoned-Day embodiment of khushūʿ.
In the Day's terror, eyes are خَاشِعَةٌ; the visual humility parallels 88:2 while 20:108 supplies its silenced sound.
The righteous are told to enter the gardens in peace and security, placing salām at Paradise's threshold even though the ayah frames it as entry speech rather than reported hearing.
“Enter it in peace” is the enduring Day's welcome, another wholesome utterance marking admission to Paradise.
The people of the Heights call “Peace be upon you” to the Garden's people; the greeting is Paradise-directed, though its speakers have not yet entered.
When the ignorant address the Merciful's servants, they answer “peace”; an earthly encounter turns hostile or foolish speech into the very word heard in Paradise.
Believers must not raise their voices above the Prophet's or shout speech at him, making vocal restraint part of proper reception of the messenger.
Those who lower their voices before God's Messenger are praised for tested hearts, a voluntary earthly humility in sound beside the involuntary hush before the Merciful.
The warning text is itself a تَذْكِرَةٌ, identifying revelation by the work that 88:21 commissions the Prophet to perform.
Whoever wills may remember it, locating the response to the reminder of 74:54 in the hearer's own reception.
The revelation is called a تَذْكِرَةٌ, another direct description of the message as an awakening reminder.
Whoever wills may remember it, completing the movement from an offered reminder to memory in its recipient.
“This is a reminder” and whoever wills may take a way to his Lord; the heard warning opens a route but does not compel the hearer.
The repeated declaration that the revelation is a reminder leaves taking the way to God to the willing listener.
The Prophet is commanded to remind despite accusations of soothsaying or madness, preserving his speaking role amid hostile reception.
The Prophet must leave those who turn religion into play yet remind with the revelation lest a soul be delivered to ruin, joining noncontrol with continued warning.
Moses is told to bring his people from darkness and remind them of God's days, making narrated divine acts an oral warning for a community.
The Quran is made easy in the Prophet's tongue so he can give good news and warn, supporting the section's account of ذكر as something voiced for others.
The Prophet is told that when God recites the revelation he should follow its recitation, showing the first messenger as a listener before he becomes its voice.
The people of the Fire are ordered to remain despised and not speak to God, a punitive eschatological silence distinct from both Paradise's pure speech and Judgment's general hush.
The people of Hell are reminded that they lived long enough for one who would remember and that a warner came, so belated pleading is answered by the report they ignored.
Hell's keepers ask whether messengers came with clear proofs; the condemned admit they did, again measuring the realized scene against previously delivered warning.
No word is uttered without a watcher ready to record it; spoken words do not vanish but become part of the account that closes surah 88.
Those plotting are asked whether God does not hear their secrets and private counsel, while messengers record it; apparently unheard speech still enters the final record.
The people are said scarcely to understand any حَدِيثًا, using discourse together with failed comprehension and thereby supporting the section's distinction between hearing words and grasping them.
Lowering the voice is urged because the harshest voices are donkeys' voices; this is an analogical parallel to the dictionary's animal-noise branch of لغو, though the animal and root differ.
